colchis.name: Colchis
colchis.summary: An ancient region on the eastern Black Sea coast, now western Georgia, known in Greek mythology as home to the Golden Fleece and Medea and the destination of the Argonauts.

georgians.name: Georgians
georgians.summary: Caucasian ethnic group native to present-day Georgia, speaking Georgian, a language unrelated to any other known language family. They were among the first peoples to embrace Christianity, in the early 4th century.

saint-nino.name: Saint Nino
saint-nino.summary: Woman who preached Christianity in the Kingdom of Iberia, in present-day Georgia, and is credited with its Christianization. Tradition says she converted Queen Nana and King Mirian III, who declared Christianity the official religion around 326.

kartli.name: Kartli
kartli.summary: A historical region in central-to-eastern Georgia along the Mtkvari river, known to classical authors as Hiberia; it became a separate kingdom centered on Tbilisi after Georgia's 15th-century partition.

nicomedes-i-of-bithynia.name: Nicomedes I of Bithynia
nicomedes-i-of-bithynia.summary: Second king of Bithynia, eldest son of Zipoetes I, whom he succeeded on the throne in 278 BC, reigning until about 255 BC.

urartu.name: Urartu
urartu.summary: An Iron Age kingdom centered on the Armenian highlands that warred often with Assyria and became, for a time, the most powerful state in the Near East before falling in the 6th century BC.

garni-temple.name: Garni Temple
garni-temple.summary: A first-century colonnaded temple in Armenia, conventionally attributed to King Tiridates I as a shrine to the sun god Mihr, and the only largely preserved Hellenistic building in the former Soviet Union.

ionic-order.name: Ionic order
ionic-order.summary: One of the three classical architectural orders, alongside the Doric and Corinthian, identified by columns with volute-scrolled capitals and narrower columns than the Doric.

mihr-armenian-deity.name: Mihr
mihr-armenian-deity.summary: The Armenian deity of fire, son of the supreme god Aramazd, identified with the Greek god Hephaestus.

tiridates-i-of-armenia.name: Tiridates I of Armenia
tiridates-i-of-armenia.summary: King of Armenia from 53 CE and founder of its Arsacid dynasty; his crowning by Roman emperor Nero in 66 ended a long Roman-Parthian conflict over Armenia and made it a client kingdom.

temple-of-artemis.name: Temple of Artemis
temple-of-artemis.summary: A Greek temple to the goddess Artemis at Ephesus, repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt in antiquity, with worship continuing there until around 401 AD.

mausoleum-at-halicarnassus.name: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
mausoleum-at-halicarnassus.summary: A tomb built between 353 and 351 BC for Mausolus and his wife Artemisia II, decorated by four Greek sculptors and later ranked one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World until earthquakes destroyed it.

mausolus.name: Mausolus
mausolus.summary: Ruler of Caria from 377 to 353 BCE and a satrap of the Achaemenid Empire, who also held Lycia and parts of Ionia and is best known for his monumental tomb.

artemisia-ii-of-caria.name: Artemisia II
artemisia-ii-of-caria.summary: A naval strategist who succeeded her brother-husband Mausolus as ruler of Caria, reigning from 353 to 351 BC and remembered for her grief-stricken devotion to him.

satyros.name: Satyros of Paros
satyros.summary: A 4th-century BC Greek architect and sculptor from Paros who, with Pythius of Priene, designed the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

pythius-of-priene.name: Pythius of Priene
pythius-of-priene.summary: 4th-century BC Greek architect and sculptor who designed the Temple of Athena Polias at Priene and the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

mount-nemrut.name: Mount Nemrut
mount-nemrut.summary: Mountain in southeastern Turkey topped by large 1st-century-BC statues around a royal tomb, made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.

antiochus-i-of-commagene.name: Antiochus I of Commagene
antiochus-i-of-commagene.summary: King of the Greco-Iranian kingdom of Commagene (ruled 70–31 BC) known for the tomb-sanctuary he built atop Mount Nemrut, a UNESCO World Heritage site.

commagene.name: Commagene
commagene.summary: An ancient Greco-Iranian kingdom centred on the city of Samosata, ruled by a Hellenized branch of the Orontid dynasty and often called a buffer state between Rome, Parthia, Armenia and Syria.

tiridates-iii-of-armenia.name: Tiridates III of Armenia
tiridates-iii-of-armenia.summary: Armenian Arsacid king from about 298 to 330 who adopted Christianity as Armenia's state religion around 301, making it the first state to do so officially.

gregory-the-illuminator.name: Gregory the Illuminator
gregory-the-illuminator.summary: Founder and first head of the Armenian Apostolic Church (about 257 to about 331), reputedly a Parthian nobleman's son who was imprisoned 14 years in a pit before converting King Tiridates III to Christianity.

garni-gorge.name: Garni Gorge
garni-gorge.summary: A gorge near Yerevan, Armenia, known for basalt-column cliff walls called the 'Symphony of the Stones' and overlooked by the first-century Temple of Garni.

geghard.name: Geghard Monastery
geghard.summary: A medieval monastery in Armenia, partly carved out of a mountain, founded in the 4th century and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

chersiphron.name: Chersiphron
chersiphron.summary: A Greek architect from Knossos in Crete (6th century BC) who, with his son Metagenes, began a new Temple of Artemis at Ephesus around 550 BC, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

croesus.name: Croesus
croesus.summary: Last king of Lydia (585–546 BC), famed for his great wealth, who was defeated by the Persian king Cyrus the Great after the siege of his capital, Sardis.

herostratus.name: Herostratus
herostratus.summary: An obscure man who burned down the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus in 356 BCE purely to gain lasting fame, giving rise to a term for crimes committed just for notoriety.

leochares.name: Leochares
leochares.summary: An ancient Greek sculptor from Athens active in the 4th century BC.

bryaxis.name: Bryaxis
bryaxis.summary: Greek sculptor active around 350 BC who created the reliefs on one side of the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, built for the ruler Mausolus.

scopas.name: Scopas
scopas.summary: An ancient Greek sculptor and architect from Paros, active in the 4th century BC, most famous for his statue of Meleager, a copper statue of Aphrodite, and the head of the goddess Hygieia.

timotheus-sculptor.name: Timotheus
timotheus-sculptor.summary: Greek sculptor of the 4th century BC who worked on the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus and is credited with a famous sculpture of Leda and the Swan.

polykleitos.name: Polykleitos
polykleitos.summary: A 5th-century BCE Greek sculptor ranked among the greatest of classical antiquity, famous for a lost treatise setting out ideal proportions for the male body; no originals survive, only later copies.

kresilas.name: Kresilas
kresilas.summary: Greek sculptor (about 480–410 BC) from Kydonia who worked in Athens during the Peloponnesian War, best known for his statue of Pericles.

phradmon.name: Phradmon
phradmon.summary: A little-known ancient Greek sculptor from Argos, said by Pliny to have placed fifth in a contest to sculpt a Wounded Amazon, and credited with a statue of an Olympic victor and a bronze group dedicated to Athena Itonia.

pausanias-geographer.name: Pausanias (geographer)
pausanias-geographer.summary: A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer, c. 110 to 180, whose Description of Greece is a key source linking classical literature to archaeological sites.

artemis.name: Artemis
artemis.summary: The Greek goddess of hunting, wilderness and childbirth, daughter of Zeus and Leto and twin sister of Apollo.

nyx.name: Nyx
nyx.summary: The Greek goddess and personification of Night, one of the first deities to exist in early cosmogonies; even Zeus is said to have feared displeasing her.

rhoecus.name: Rhoecus
rhoecus.summary: Greek sculptor from Samos in the 6th century BCE, noted with his son for work in bronze, credited with building the Temple of Hera at Samos and a marble figure of Night at the Temple of Artemis, Ephesus.

delian-league.name: Delian League
delian-league.summary: A confederacy of Greek city-states founded in 478 BC under Athenian leadership to continue fighting Persia after the victory at Plataea; it later became an Athenian naval empire.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

mithridates-vi-eupator.name: Mithridates VI Eupator
mithridates-vi-eupator.summary: Hellenistic ruler of the Kingdom of Pontus from 120 to 63 BCE who fought several wars against Rome to dominate Anatolia and the Black Sea, ultimately unsuccessful.

kingdom-of-pontus.name: Kingdom of Pontus
kingdom-of-pontus.summary: A Hellenistic kingdom on the Black Sea coast of northern Anatolia, founded in 281 BCE and ruled by a Persian-descended dynasty, reaching its height under Mithridates VI before Rome's conquest in 63 BCE.

mithridatic-wars.name: Mithridatic Wars
mithridatic-wars.summary: Three conflicts between 88 and 63 BCE between the Roman Republic and King Mithridates VI of Pontus, ending with Rome annexing Pontus and Syria after his death.

galatia.name: Galatia
galatia.summary: An ancient region in the highlands of central Anatolia, named after Gauls from Thrace who settled there in the 3rd century BC after invading the Balkans in 279 BC.

bithynia.name: Bithynia
bithynia.summary: A region of northwestern Asia Minor that was an independent Hellenistic kingdom from the 3rd century BCE before passing to Rome in 74 BCE.

zipoetes-ii-of-bithynia.name: Zipoetes II
zipoetes-ii-of-bithynia.summary: Ruler of Bithynia from 279 to 276 BCE.

seleucid-empire.name: Seleucid Empire
seleucid-empire.summary: A Greek state in West Asia founded by Seleucus I Nicator in 312 BC after Alexander the Great's empire divided, ruling from Seleucia and Antioch until Rome annexed it in 63 BC.

battle-of-magnesia.name: Battle of Magnesia
battle-of-magnesia.summary: 190 or 189 BC battle in which Rome and its ally Pergamon decisively defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III, leading to the treaty that ended Seleucid rule in Asia Minor.

kingdom-of-pergamon.name: Kingdom of Pergamon
kingdom-of-pergamon.summary: A Greek Hellenistic kingdom ruling western Asia Minor from its capital Pergamon, founded when Philetaerus rebelled against Lysimachus in 281 BCE and lasting until Rome absorbed it around 129 BCE.

rhodes.name: Rhodes
rhodes.summary: The largest of Greece's Dodecanese islands, historically ruled by the Knights of Saint John from 1310 to 1522 and home to the ancient Colossus of Rhodes.

battle-of-pteria.name: Battle of Pteria
battle-of-pteria.summary: An indecisive 547 BC battle in Cappadocia between Cyrus the Great's Persian forces and King Croesus of Lydia, with heavy losses on both sides; Cyrus later defeated Croesus decisively at Thymbra.

battle-of-thymbra.name: Battle of Thymbra
battle-of-thymbra.summary: The decisive 547 BC battle in which Cyrus II of Persia defeated the much larger army of Croesus of Lydia, leading to the siege and fall of the Lydian capital Sardis.

cyrus-the-great.name: Cyrus the Great
cyrus-the-great.summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire (c. 600–530 BC), who conquered the Median, Lydian and Neo-Babylonian empires to create the largest empire of its time, known for tolerating local customs and religions.

lydia.name: Lydia
lydia.summary: A wealthy Iron Age kingdom of western Anatolia (8th–6th centuries BC), capital Sardis, credited with the world's first coinage, which became a Persian satrapy in 546 BC.

ionian-revolt.name: Ionian Revolt
ionian-revolt.summary: A rebellion of Greek cities in Asia Minor against Persian rule (499–493 BCE), triggered by dissatisfaction with Persian-appointed tyrants and marked by the burning of Sardis in 498 BCE.

aristagoras.name: Aristagoras
aristagoras.summary: Tyrant of the Greek city of Miletus in the late 6th and early 5th centuries BC who helped instigate the Ionian Revolt against the Persian Achaemenid Empire.

sardis.name: Sardis
sardis.summary: An ancient city in what is now Turkey, capital of the Lydian Empire and later of a Persian satrapy, now an active archaeological site and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

darius-the-great.name: Darius the Great
darius-the-great.summary: Third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire (522–486 BCE), who ruled it at its territorial peak, reorganized it into provinces, and commissioned the Behistun inscription.

battle-of-lade.name: Battle of Lade
battle-of-lade.summary: 494 BC naval battle in which the Persian Empire crushed an alliance of Ionian and Lesbian Greek cities, effectively ending the Ionian Revolt.

tiglath-pileser-iii.name: Tiglath-Pileser III
tiglath-pileser-iii.summary: Neo-Assyrian king (745–727 BC) who doubled Assyrian territory through brutal military reforms, marking Assyria's shift into a true empire.

cimmerians.name: Cimmerians
cimmerians.summary: An ancient Iranic nomadic people from the Pontic-Caspian steppe who migrated into West Asia, known mainly through Assyrian and later Greek and Roman records.

scythians.name: Scythians
scythians.summary: An ancient Eastern Iranic nomadic people who migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe in the 9th-8th centuries BC, dominating the region through mounted warfare before being conquered by the Sarmatians in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC.

medes.name: Medes
medes.summary: An Iron Age Iranian people who inhabited northwestern Iran from around the 11th century BCE and, according to Greek sources, formed a powerful state that helped overthrow the Assyrian Empire.

cyzicus.name: Cyzicus
cyzicus.summary: Ancient Greek town in Mysia, Anatolia (modern Turkey), located on a peninsula in the Sea of Marmara.

didyma.name: Didyma
didyma.summary: Ancient Greek sanctuary on the Ionian coast near Miletus, famed for its oracle of Apollo housed within a well-preserved Hellenistic temple.

priene.name: Priene
priene.summary: An ancient Greek city of Ionia near the Maeander River, known for high-quality Hellenistic art and architecture though never politically significant due to its small size.

thyatira.name: Thyatira
thyatira.summary: An ancient Greek city in Asia Minor, now the Turkish city of Akhisar, located in far western Turkey near the Aegean Sea.

artaphernes.name: Artaphernes
artaphernes.summary: A brother of Achaemenid king Darius I who governed as satrap of Lydia from about 513 to 492 BC and helped suppress the Ionian Revolt.

satrap.name: Satrap
satrap.summary: A provincial governor in the ancient Persian and later Hellenistic and Sasanian empires, acting as a semi-autonomous viceroy; the word later came to mean a corrupt or tyrannical local ruler.

esarhaddon.name: Esarhaddon
esarhaddon.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (681–669 BCE), famous for conquering Egypt in 671 BCE and for rebuilding Babylon after his father had destroyed it.

ashurbanipal.name: Ashurbanipal
ashurbanipal.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 to 631 BC, often called the last great Assyrian king, whose 38-year reign marked both the empire's height and the start of its decline.

caria.name: Caria
caria.summary: A region of western Anatolia along the coast, stretching from mid-Ionia south to Lycia and east to Phrygia, home to the Carian-speaking people.

cilicia.name: Cilicia
cilicia.summary: A geographical region of southern Anatolia along the Mediterranean coast, historically bordering Pamphylia, Cappadocia and Syria, now covering Turkey's Mersin, Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay provinces.

gyges-of-lydia.name: Gyges of Lydia
gyges-of-lydia.summary: Founder of the Mermnad dynasty of Lydian kings, reigning around 680–644 BC, and the first Lydian ruler to try building it into a powerful empire.

candaules.name: Candaules
candaules.summary: A 7th-century BC king of the ancient kingdom of Lydia, said by Herodotus to have been betrayed and killed by his own wife, ending the Heraclid dynasty he belonged to.

phrygia.name: Phrygia
phrygia.summary: A civilization and kingdom in west-central Anatolia centered on the Sangarios River, which reached its peak under King Midas in the late 8th century BC before falling to Cimmerian raiders and later Lydian, Persian and Hellenistic rule.

gordion.name: Gordium
gordion.summary: Ancient capital of Phrygia, near modern Ankara, Turkey, inhabited from around 2300 BCE and famous for the Gordian Knot and its Iron Age burial mounds.

antiochus-i-soter.name: Antiochus I Soter
antiochus-i-soter.summary: Greco-Sogdian Seleucid king (c. 324/3–261 BC) who succeeded his father Seleucus I Nicator in 281 BC and overcame a period of instability during his reign.

sennacherib.name: Sennacherib
sennacherib.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BC, famed in the Hebrew Bible for his Levant campaign, who destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and expanded the capital Nineveh.

palaic-language.name: Palaic
palaic-language.summary: An extinct Indo-European language recorded on Bronze Age cuneiform tablets in the Hittite capital Hattusa, likely spoken in northern Anatolia until around the 15th century BCE.

luwian-language.name: Luwian language
luwian-language.summary: An ancient Indo-European language, or group of languages, of Anatolia, written in cuneiform or hieroglyphic scripts and named after the region of Luwiya.

isaurian-language.name: Isaurian language
isaurian-language.summary: Extinct language spoken in Isauria, Asia Minor, attested in inscriptions into the 6th century AD, with personal names showing Luwian, Indo-European roots.

koine-greek.name: Koine Greek
koine-greek.summary: The common form of Greek spoken and written across the Hellenistic world, Roman Empire and early Byzantine Empire, spreading after Alexander the Great's conquests and used for the Septuagint and New Testament.

late-bronze-age-collapse.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
late-bronze-age-collapse.summary: A sudden societal collapse across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, ending major Bronze Age powers like the Hittite Empire.

hattusa.name: Hattusa
hattusa.summary: Capital of the Hittite Empire in the late Bronze Age, in modern Turkey; its ruins were rediscovered in 1834 and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

lycian-language.name: Lycian language
lycian-language.summary: The extinct language of the ancient Lycians of Anatolia, mostly recorded in 5th–4th century BC inscriptions using its own Greek-related alphabet, before dying out around the 1st century BC.

lydian-language.name: Lydian language
lydian-language.summary: An extinct Indo-European Anatolian language spoken in Lydia, attested from about the 8th–7th century BC to the 3rd century BC, with its best-preserved texts from the 5th–4th centuries BC.

carian-language.name: Carian language
carian-language.summary: An extinct Anatolian language spoken by the Carians, closely related to Lycian and Luwian, known mainly from about 170 inscriptions found in Egypt.

sidetic-language.name: Sidetic language
sidetic-language.summary: Extinct Anatolian branch of Indo-European known from coin legends and bilingual inscriptions from the city of Side, dating to the 5th-2nd centuries BCE, likely related to Lydian, Carian and Lycian.

pisidian-language.name: Pisidian
pisidian-language.summary: An extinct Anatolian language of ancient Asia Minor, known from about fifty short inscriptions from the 1st and 2nd centuries AD and closely related to Lycian.

solymoi.name: Solymoi
solymoi.summary: An ancient people of the mountainous interior of southwestern Anatolia, first mentioned in Greek epic as opponents of the hero Bellerophon; their exact identity is debated.

bellerophon.name: Bellerophon
bellerophon.summary: A hero of Greek mythology, son of Poseidon, famed for slaying the monster Chimera and taming the winged horse Pegasus.

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

hittite-language.name: Hittite language
hittite-language.summary: An extinct Indo-European language spoken in Bronze Age Anatolia, attested in cuneiform texts from the 17th to 13th centuries BC and among the earliest recorded Indo-European languages.

gordias.name: Gordias
gordias.summary: Legendary founder of the Phrygian capital Gordium, maker of the Gordian Knot, and father of King Midas, placed by legend sometime in the 2nd millennium BC.

gordian-knot.name: Gordian Knot
gordian-knot.summary: A legendary, seemingly impossible knot at Gordium that Alexander the Great famously cut with his sword in 333 BC instead of untying, becoming a symbol of unconventional solutions.

midas.name: Midas
midas.summary: Legendary Phrygian king remembered for the golden touch; a historical Midas ruling in the late 8th century BC is likely the Mita who warred with Assyria.

mygdon.name: Mygdon of Phrygia
mygdon.summary: A legendary king of Phrygia in Greek mythology who allied with King Priam of Troy.

alwin-kloekhorst.name: Alwin Kloekhorst
alwin-kloekhorst.summary: A Dutch linguist, Indo-Europeanist and Hittitologist, born in 1978, appointed a full professor in Anatolian Linguistics at Leiden University in 2023.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

strabo.name: Strabo
strabo.summary: Greek geographer (64/63 BC to about 24 AD) best known for his Geographica, a descriptive survey of the peoples and places known in his time.

pliny-the-elder.name: Pliny the Elder
pliny-the-elder.summary: A Roman author, naturalist and military commander (23/24–79 AD) who wrote the 37-volume encyclopedia Natural History and died attempting to rescue people during the eruption of Vesuvius.

milyas.name: Milyas
milyas.summary: A mountainous region in ancient south-west Anatolia, generally placed within Lycia, Pisidia and Phrygia, whose boundaries Herodotus said were never fixed.

termessos.name: Termessos
termessos.summary: A well-preserved ancient Pisidian city built high in the Taurus Mountains of Turkey, founded by the Solymi and later integrated into the Greek world after Alexander the Great's conquests.

sabazios.name: Sabazios
sabazios.summary: A sky-father and horseman deity originating in Asia Minor, worshipped by the Phrygians and Thracians and later identified by the Greeks with Zeus or Dionysus.

hipparchus.name: Hipparchus
hipparchus.summary: A Greek astronomer, geographer and mathematician (c. 190–120 BC) considered the founder of trigonometry, famous for discovering the precession of the equinoxes and often called the father of astronomy.

nicaea.name: Nicaea
nicaea.summary: An ancient Greek city in northwestern Anatolia, site of the first and seventh Ecumenical Councils and source of the Nicene Creed, later capital of the Empire of Nicaea and briefly of the Ottomans.

axial-precession.name: Precession of the equinoxes
axial-precession.summary: The slow, continuous shift in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis over a roughly 26,000-year cycle, historically called the precession of the equinoxes.

apollonius-of-perga.name: Apollonius of Perga
apollonius-of-perga.summary: An ancient Greek geometer and astronomer (c. 240-190 BC) who named the ellipse, parabola and hyperbola and is ranked among antiquity's greatest mathematicians.

perga.name: Perga
perga.summary: An ancient city in Pamphylia, now in Turkey, that became capital of a Roman province and was the birthplace of the mathematician Apollonius.

pamphylia.name: Pamphylia
pamphylia.summary: A region on the south coast of Asia Minor, between Lycia and Cilicia, in what is now Antalya province, Turkey.

euclid.name: Euclid
euclid.summary: An ancient Greek mathematician active around 300 BC, called the 'father of geometry' for his treatise Elements, which dominated the field of geometry until the 19th century.

archimedes.name: Archimedes
archimedes.summary: Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist and engineer from Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), regarded as one of the greatest mathematicians of all time for his work on geometry, levers and buoyancy.

geographica.name: Geographica
geographica.summary: A 17-book encyclopedia of geographical knowledge written in Greek in the late first century BC, attributed to the geographer Strabo, describing the known ancient world.

tiberius.name: Tiberius
tiberius.summary: Second Roman emperor, ruling from AD 14 to 37 as Augustus's stepson and successor, and earlier one of Rome's most successful generals.

kingdom-of-kush.name: Kingdom of Kush
kingdom-of-kush.summary: An ancient kingdom in Nubia along the Nile in what is now Sudan and Egypt, rising from the city-state of Kerma and later ruling Egypt itself in the 8th century BCE under King Piye.

philae-temple-complex.name: Philae
philae-temple-complex.summary: An island-based temple complex on the Nile near Aswan, Egypt, dismantled and relocated in the 1960s–70s to save it from flooding by the new Aswan Dam.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Founder of the Roman Empire, ruling as its first emperor from 27 BC until his death in AD 14, and known earlier as Octavian.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

attalus-ii-philadelphus.name: Attalus II Philadelphus
attalus-ii-philadelphus.summary: Ruler of the Attalid kingdom of Pergamon from 220 to 138 BC and founder of the city of Attalia.

eumenes-ii.name: Eumenes II
eumenes-ii.summary: King of the Hellenistic kingdom of Pergamon from 197 to 159 BC, son of Attalus I and Queen Apollonis and a member of the Attalid dynasty.

pergamon.name: Pergamon
pergamon.summary: A powerful ancient Greek city in Anatolia, capital of the Hellenistic Kingdom of Pergamon under the Attalid dynasty, known for its acropolis and famous altar.

nebuchadnezzar-ii.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
nebuchadnezzar-ii.summary: Second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling 605 to 562 BC; renowned for military victories including Carchemish and for major construction projects in Babylon.

astyages.name: Astyages
astyages.summary: Last king of the Median kingdom, reigning from 585 to 550 BCE. He was the son of Cyaxares and was dethroned by the Persian king Cyrus the Great.

cyaxares.name: Cyaxares
cyaxares.summary: Third king of the Medes, who took the throne in 625 BC, overthrew Scythian domination, and allied with Babylon to destroy the Assyrian Empire, turning Media into a major power.

alyattes.name: Alyattes
alyattes.summary: Fourth king of Lydia's Mermnad dynasty, reigning about 635 to 585 BC, sometimes credited as the first ruler to issue coins, made from electrum.

aryenis.name: Aryenis
aryenis.summary: Daughter of the Lydian king Alyattes and sister of King Croesus, according to Herodotus.

kingdom-of-cappadocia.name: Kingdom of Cappadocia
kingdom-of-cappadocia.summary: A Hellenistic-era kingdom in central Anatolia formed from a former Persian province, ruled by three royal houses over three centuries until it became a Roman province in 17 AD.

ariobarzanes-iii-of-cappadocia.name: Ariobarzanes III of Cappadocia
ariobarzanes-iii-of-cappadocia.summary: King of Cappadocia from about 51 to 42 BC, of Persian and Greek descent, who backed Pompey and was executed in 42 BC for resisting Roman control.

ariarathes-x-of-cappadocia.name: Ariarathes X of Cappadocia
ariarathes-x-of-cappadocia.summary: King of Cappadocia from about 42 to 36 BC, of Persian and Greek descent, who took the throne after his brother's death but was soon removed and executed by Mark Antony.

mark-antony.name: Mark Antony
mark-antony.summary: Roman politician and general (83–30 BC) and ally of Julius Caesar who, after Caesar's assassination, formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and later allied with Cleopatra.

archelaus-of-cappadocia.name: Archelaus of Cappadocia
archelaus-of-cappadocia.summary: Roman client prince and the last king of Cappadocia, who died in 17 AD; husband of Pythodorida, Queen regnant of Pontus.

sargon-ii.name: Sargon II
sargon-ii.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 722 to 705 BC who expanded Assyrian territory, built a new capital called Dur-Sharrukin, and modeled his reign on legendary ancient rulers.

ionia.name: Ionia
ionia.summary: An ancient region on the central western coast of Anatolia settled by Greek Ionians, home to twelve cities of the Ionian League and central to conflicts between Persia and Greece.

battle-of-actium.name: Battle of Actium
battle-of-actium.summary: A naval battle fought on 2 September 31 BCE in which Octavian's fleet, aided by Marcus Agrippa, defeated the combined forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra, the climax of their long rivalry.

heracleidae.name: Heraclidae
heracleidae.summary: Mythical descendants of the hero Heracles, a group of Dorian kings said to have conquered Mycenae, Sparta and Argos and later claimed as ancestors by several historical dynasties.

mushki.name: Mushki
mushki.summary: Iron Age people of Anatolia known from Assyrian sources, split into an eastern group near the Euphrates and a later western group identified with the Phrygians.

diocletian.name: Diocletian
diocletian.summary: Roman emperor from 284 to 305 who ended the Crisis of the Third Century and began splitting the empire by creating the Tetrarchy, sharing rule with three co-emperors.

tetrarchy.name: Tetrarchy
tetrarchy.summary: The system devised by Emperor Diocletian to rule the Roman Empire through two senior emperors and two junior successors, in place from 293 to 324 CE.

miletus.name: Miletus
miletus.summary: Ancient Greek city on Anatolia's western coast, a wealthy maritime and trading power that founded dozens of Mediterranean and Black Sea colonies and was home to early philosophers such as Thales; known in Hittite records as Millawata.

ionian-school-philosophy.name: Milesian school
ionian-school-philosophy.summary: The group of early Ionian philosophers—Thales, Anaximander, and Anaximenes—based in Miletus, who sought nature's basic underlying element through abstract reasoning rather than experiment.

thales-of-miletus.name: Thales of Miletus
thales-of-miletus.summary: A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus, c. 626-548 BC, often called the first philosopher for explaining nature without myth; he held that everything derives from water.

anaximander.name: Anaximander
anaximander.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher of Miletus (c. 610–c. 546 BC), the first known to write down his studies, who proposed the apeiron as the source of all things and created an early map of the world.

anaximenes-of-miletus.name: Anaximenes
anaximenes-of-miletus.summary: A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher from Miletus (c. 586/585–526/525 BC), the last of the three Milesian School thinkers, who held that air was the basic element from which all things form.

pre-socratic-philosophy.name: Pre-Socratic philosophy
pre-socratic-philosophy.summary: Ancient Greek philosophy before Socrates, beginning in the 6th century BC, which sought to explain the origin and nature of the universe through natural law rather than the gods.

lydian-religion.name: Lydian religion
lydian-religion.summary: The mythology, rituals and beliefs of the ancient Lydians of Iron Age Anatolia, centred, on limited evidence, around the fertility of nature.

apeiron.name: Apeiron
apeiron.summary: An ancient Greek word for the unlimited or boundless, used by the philosopher Anaximander to describe the origin of the world.

xenophanes.name: Xenophanes
xenophanes.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher and poet (c. 570-478 BC) known for satirical verse criticizing Homer's gods and for seeking natural explanations of phenomena without myth.

heraclitus.name: Heraclitus
heraclitus.summary: Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher (flourished c. 500 BC) from Ephesus known for the idea that everything is in constant flux, as in "no man ever steps in the same river twice."

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras
pythagoras.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (c. 570–495 BC) from Samos, founder of Pythagoreanism, later credited with the Pythagorean theorem and the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

kamru-epa.name: Kamrušepa
kamru-epa.summary: A Hittite and Luwian goddess of medicine and magic, best known for her role in the Telepinu Myth in pacifying an angry vegetation god.

luwians.name: Luwians
luwians.summary: An ancient Anatolian people who spoke the Luwian language, part of the Hittite Empire in the Bronze Age and later founders of Neo-Hittite states in northern Syria.

list-of-kings-of-lydia.name: Mermnad dynasty
list-of-kings-of-lydia.summary: The historical royal dynasty of ancient Lydia in western Anatolia, following the legendary Maeoniae and Heracleidae lines described by Herodotus.

tiwaz-luwian-deity.name: Tiwaz
tiwaz-luwian-deity.summary: The Luwian Sun-god, one of the most important deities of the Luwians, sometimes given the epithet 'father'.

sun-goddess-of-arinna.name: Sun goddess of Arinna
sun-goddess-of-arinna.summary: The chief goddess of Hittite mythology and protector of the Hittite kingdom, called 'Queen of all lands' and worshipped with the weather god Tarḫunna at the sacred city of Arinna.

arslantepe.name: Arslantepe
arslantepe.summary: An ancient city, also known as Melid, on a tributary of the upper Euphrates near modern Malatya, Turkey; a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

illuyanka.name: Illuyanka
illuyanka.summary: A serpentine dragon in Hittite mythology slain by the storm god Tarhunz, known from cuneiform tablets linked to a spring festival ritual at the Hittite capital Hattusa.

typhon.name: Typhon
typhon.summary: Monstrous serpentine giant in Greek mythology, son of Gaia and Tartarus, who fought Zeus for control of the cosmos and was ultimately defeated and imprisoned.

tud-aliya-iv.name: Tudḫaliya IV
tud-aliya-iv.summary: King of the Hittite Empire who reigned around 1245 to 1215 BC, son of Ḫattušili III and Queen Puduḫepa.

tar-unta-a.name: Tarḫuntašša
tar-unta-a.summary: A Bronze Age Anatolian city of unknown location that served for a time as capital of the Hittite Empire before becoming a regional power in its own right.

proto-indo-european-mythology.name: Proto-Indo-European mythology
proto-indo-european-mythology.summary: The reconstructed body of myths and gods of the Proto-Indo-Europeans, inferred from shared elements across Indo-European traditions, including a sky father and dawn goddess.

ancient-mesopotamian-religion.name: Mesopotamian religion
ancient-mesopotamian-religion.summary: The religious beliefs and practices of Sumer, Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia from roughly 6000 BC to 500 AD, centered on worship of the forces of nature as providers of sustenance.

lycians.name: Lycians
lycians.summary: Name for various peoples who lived at different times in Lycia, a region of Anatolia also known as Asia Minor.

lycia.name: Lycia
lycia.summary: An ancient region of Anatolia populated by Luwic speakers, known from Late Bronze Age Egyptian and Hittite records; it later passed under Persian, Greek and Macedonian control.

carians.name: Carians
carians.summary: The ancient inhabitants of Caria in southwest Anatolia, who spoke the Carian language.

anatolian-hieroglyphs.name: Anatolian hieroglyphs
anatolian-hieroglyphs.summary: An indigenous logographic script of about 500 signs native to central Anatolia, encoding the Luwian language and once mistakenly called Hittite hieroglyphs.
